name: Five Whys
use_case: An iterative root-cause technique that asks 'why did that happen?' repeatedly against a single observed failure until the answer stops being a symptom and starts being a fixable cause. Best used right after an incident, an outage, a recurring defect, or a missed deadline, when the team can describe what went wrong but keeps fixing the surface rather than the underlying condition that produced it.
strengths: needs no tooling, template, or facilitator training
keeps a single failure in focus instead of drifting into general complaints
exposes process and system causes that a blame-first discussion hides
fast enough to run inside an existing incident review
weaknesses: follows one causal chain, so parallel contributing causes get dropped
quality depends entirely on the participants' knowledge of the system
stops wherever the group runs out of insight, which may be short of the real cause
invites a plausible narrative that nobody verifies against evidence
use_cases: A council benefits office keeps sending letters with the wrong payment date, and each correction to the template has failed to stop the next batch going out wrong.
A packaging line keeps halting on the same jam; operators clear it every time and the shift supervisor wants to find the condition upstream that keeps producing it.
A GP practice sent a referral that never reached the hospital, and the practice team wants to trace which administrative step let it slip before it happens to another patient.
A school literacy team sees reading results in one year group stall despite a new intervention, and wants to get past blaming pupil motivation to what in its own support system is not working.
Complaints about late deliveries keep arriving from one region, and the operations manager wants the frontline team to follow one concrete late order back to where it went wrong.
